roles: member of the Safed mystical circle
summary: Solomon ben Moses ha-Levi Alkabetz (c. 1500-1576) was a kabbalist and liturgical poet of the sixteenth-century Safed circle, best known as the author of Lekha Dodi ('Come, my beloved'), the hymn welcoming the Sabbath that became a fixed part of the Kabbalat Shabbat liturgy. He was the teacher and brother-in-law of Moses Cordovero, who married Alkabetz's sister, and is associated with the Safed custom of going out into the fields at dusk on Friday to receive the Sabbath as a bride. He also composed kabbalistic and homiletical works, and signed Lekha Dodi with an acrostic spelling his name, Shlomo ha-Levi, in the initial letters of its stanzas.
description:
Solomon ben Moses ha-Levi Alkabetz, born about 1500 (in the accounts, at Salonica or in its region), settled in Safed (Tzfat) in the Galilee, the sixteenth-century centre of kabbalistic activity, where he belonged to the circle of mystics gathered there in the generations around Joseph Karo, Moses Cordovero, and later Isaac Luria. He is recorded in the tradition as a teacher of Cordovero and as his brother-in-law, Cordovero having married Alkabetz's sister, and he died in Safed about 1576.

Alkabetz is best known as the author of the hymn Lekha Dodi ('Come, my beloved'), composed in Safed and adopted into the Friday-evening liturgy of Kabbalat Shabbat ('receiving the Sabbath'), where it is sung across the Jewish world to the present. Its refrain, confirmed in the open text on Sefaria, runs 'Lekha dodi likrat kallah, penei Shabbat neqabbelah' ('Come, my beloved, to meet the bride; the face of the Sabbath let us receive'), taking up the tradition, traced in the accounts to the Safed kabbalists and to a rabbinic image, of greeting the Sabbath as a bride and a queen: on the custom associated with the circle, the mystics would go out into the fields toward dusk on Friday to receive the Sabbath. The nine body stanzas of the hymn are signed with an acrostic: the initial letters of eight of them spell the poet's name, Shlomo ha-Levi, a signature confirmed verbatim in the Sefaria text (the stanzas open with the letters shin, lamed, mem, he, he, lamed, vav, yod). The hymn weaves together the theme of the Sabbath as bride with the messianic and national longing for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the ingathering of Israel, addressing the city and the people ('Rouse yourself, rouse yourself... arise, shine, for your light has come'), and this entry reports the hymn's imagery as Alkabetz's composition and as the tradition's, not as claims the editor affirms.

Beyond the hymn, Alkabetz composed a number of kabbalistic and homiletical works, among them commentaries and mystical expositions of biblical books read at the festivals (in the accounts, on the Song of Songs, Ruth, Esther, and other texts), and he is remembered, with Karo, in connection with the practice of nocturnal study-vigils in the Safed circle. Scholarship on the Kabbalat Shabbat liturgy, chiefly the study of Reuven Kimelman, reads Lekha Dodi as a carefully constructed mystical poem whose language of the Sabbath bride carries the kabbalistic theme of the union of the divine with the Shekhinah, and this kabbalistic reading is given here as the interpretation of the poem in the tradition and in the scholarship, described and attributed rather than affirmed.

This entry presents Solomon Alkabetz on the tradition's own terms as a poet and kabbalist of the Safed circle, the author of Lekha Dodi, and the teacher and brother-in-law of Cordovero, with his poetry and its kabbalistic reading attributed to him and to the scholarship, and the primary hymn text auditable on open Sefaria.
